title: Variables, controls, sample size, reliability and validity
blurb: Identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables, spot the control group and the flaw in a design, and tell reliability from validity.
question: Researchers give 100 volunteers a caffeinated drink and 100 others an identical decaf drink, then time their reactions. Which is the independent variable, which is the dependent variable, which group is the control, and what makes the result trustworthy?

teach.h: A fair test changes one thing
teach.body: Formally, a controlled experiment deliberately changes one factor (the independent variable), measures its effect on another (the dependent variable) and holds everything else constant. In plain English: change one thing, measure what happens, keep the rest identical. Then, if the outcome differs between groups, the change you made is the only reasonable cause.

teach.caption: Ask: 'What did the experimenter choose?' (independent) and 'What did they measure?' (dependent).

teach.body: The control group does not receive the treatment (or gets a placebo or the standard condition): it is the baseline. Experimental groups receive the treatment, often at different levels. A confounding variable is an uncontrolled factor that also affects the dependent variable, so you cannot tell which factor caused the result. Changing two things at once creates a confound by design.

teach.body: Jordan, a nursing applicant in a psychology lab, helps run a study. 200 volunteers are randomly assigned: half drink caffeinated coffee, half an identical decaf (placebo). Neither the volunteers nor the staff timing them know who got which: double-blind. IV: caffeine (yes or no). DV: reaction time. Controlled: time of day, drink volume, the same computer test. The decaf group is the control. A large, randomly assigned sample with repeated trials makes the result reliable.

teach.text: The exam's favorite swaps: IV and DV reversed ('plant height' is the outcome, not the thing changed); the control GROUP confused with controlled VARIABLES; reliability (consistency) confused with validity (measuring the right thing); and a small, one-off study treated as conclusive.

items: IV: changed by the experimenter, x-axis. DV: measured, responds, y-axis. Controlled: kept the same.
Change one IV at a time; an uncontrolled factor that affects the DV is a confounding variable.
Control group: no treatment or a placebo, the baseline for comparison.
Double-blind: neither subjects nor outcome measurers know the groups. Random assignment makes groups comparable.
Reliability = consistency (repeat trials, larger sample). Validity = tests what it claims.
Only a controlled experiment can show cause and effect. Line graph for change over time.

summary: You can now name the independent, dependent and controlled variables in any experiment, identify the control group and the bias-reducing features of a design, and spot a confounding variable. You can also distinguish reliability from validity and choose the right study type and graph.

A.q: A student measures how tall tomato plants grow when given 0, 5, 10 or 15 g of fertilizer per week. What is the dependent variable?
options: The amount of fertilizer
The height of the plants
The variety of tomato
The group given no fertilizer
A.why: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change: plant height.

whyNot.0: Fertilizer is what the student deliberately changes: the independent variable.
whyNot.2: The tomato variety should be kept the same: a controlled variable.
whyNot.3: The 0 g group is the control group, not a variable.

A.q: In a trial of a new pain-relief cream, which group serves as the control group?
options: Patients given the new cream at the highest dose
Patients given the new cream twice instead of once
Patients given a look-alike cream with no drug
Patients who asked to receive the new cream
A.why: The control group does not receive the active treatment. A placebo cream gives a baseline and controls for the placebo effect.

whyNot.0: A group on the highest dose is an experimental group, not the baseline.
whyNot.1: Changing how often the cream is used is another treatment level, not a control.
whyNot.3: Self-selected patients still receive the treatment, and self-selection adds bias.

A.q: A bathroom scale reads exactly 2 kg too heavy every time the same person steps on it. Its readings are:
options: valid but not reliable
both reliable and valid
neither reliable nor valid
reliable but not valid
A.why: The readings are consistent (reliable) but do not give the true weight (not valid).

whyNot.0: This reverses the terms: the consistency makes it reliable; the offset makes it invalid.
whyNot.1: A constant 2 kg error means it does not measure the true value, so it is not valid.
whyNot.2: The readings are identical each time, so they are reliable.

B.q: Which description matches a DOUBLE-BLIND study?
options: Patients do not know whether they got the drug or placebo
Two separate groups each receive a different dose of the drug
The study is repeated twice by two independent research teams
Neither patients nor outcome assessors know who got the drug
B.why: In a double-blind design neither the subjects nor the researchers who measure outcomes know who received the treatment, which reduces bias on both sides.

whyNot.0: When only the subjects are unaware, the study is single-blind.
whyNot.1: Different doses are levels of the independent variable, not blinding.
whyNot.2: Repeating a study is replication, which improves reliability; it is not blinding.

B.q: A student tests whether music helps plants grow. The plants with music are kept by a sunny window and the plants without music in a shaded corner. What is the main flaw?
options: Plant height cannot be measured objectively
Light differs between the two groups
Music cannot serve as an independent variable
The silent plants should also have received music
B.why: Light is an uncontrolled factor that also affects growth: a confounding variable. Any difference could be due to light, not music.

whyNot.0: Height can be measured objectively with a ruler, so it is a sound dependent variable.
whyNot.2: Music (present or absent) is a perfectly testable independent variable.
whyNot.3: The silent plants are the control group; giving them music would remove the comparison.

B.q: Why are volunteers RANDOMLY ASSIGNED to the treatment and control groups?
options: To make the groups alike apart from the treatment
To make the sample represent the whole population
So that volunteers know which group they are in
To increase the number of people in the study
B.why: Random assignment spreads other differences evenly across groups, so the treatment is the main difference between them.

whyNot.1: Representing the population is the job of random SAMPLING, not random assignment.
whyNot.2: Knowing one's group would undo blinding and add bias.
whyNot.3: Assignment does not change sample size; it divides the people already recruited.

C.q: 200 volunteers are randomly assigned to drink a new sports drink or a flavored water that looks and tastes the same. Each then runs on a treadmill at the same speed and incline until exhausted, and the time is recorded. Which is a CONTROLLED variable?
options: The type of drink each group receives
The time until each volunteer is exhausted
The treadmill speed and incline used
The flavored water given to one group
C.why: Treadmill speed and incline are kept the same for everyone so they cannot explain any difference: controlled variables.

whyNot.0: The type of drink is what the researchers change: the independent variable.
whyNot.1: Time to exhaustion is what is measured: the dependent variable.
whyNot.3: The flavored water is the placebo given to the control group, not a controlled variable.

C.q: A new allergy medicine was tested once on 6 volunteers. Which change would MOST improve the reliability of the results?
options: Test many more volunteers and repeat it
Give the same 6 volunteers a larger dose
Choose volunteers who expect the drug to work
Measure a second outcome alongside the first
C.why: Larger samples and repeated trials make results consistent and less affected by chance or outliers: more reliable.

whyNot.1: A larger dose changes the treatment; it does not make the results more consistent.
whyNot.2: Choosing volunteers by expectation adds bias rather than reliability.
whyNot.3: Measuring more outcomes does not make any single result more consistent.

C.q: Which pairing of data and graph is MOST appropriate?
options: Heart rate every minute for 30 minutes: line graph
Number of students with each blood type: scatterplot
Share of a budget spent on each item: line graph
Relationship of height to arm span: pie chart
C.why: A line graph shows how a continuous variable changes over time.

whyNot.1: Counts in separate categories are compared with a bar graph.
whyNot.2: Parts of a whole are shown with a pie (circle) chart.
whyNot.3: The relationship between two numeric variables is shown with a scatterplot.

reteach.title: A fair race
reteach.question: If you wanted to know whether new running shoes make people faster, how would you set up the race so the shoes are the only possible reason for a difference?

blocks.h: Same track, same distance, different shoes
blocks.body: Give one randomly chosen group the new shoes and the other group ordinary shoes that look the same (the control). Everyone runs the same track, the same distance, on the same day (controlled variables). The shoes are the independent variable; finishing time is the dependent variable. If one group ran downhill, the hill would be a confounding variable. Race many runners, several times, and the result becomes reliable.

root.label: Do new shoes make runners faster?

blocks.text: If the new-shoe group also got extra training, you changed two things at once and can no longer credit the shoes. One independent variable at a time.

explain.body: The independent variable is changed on purpose (x-axis). The dependent variable is measured (y-axis). Controlled variables are kept the same for every group.

test.q: In a study of how water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves, which variable belongs on the y-axis?
options: Temperature of the water in °C
Mass of sugar added to each cup
Time for the sugar to dissolve
Volume of water in each cup
test.why: Dissolving time is measured in response to temperature, so it is the dependent variable, plotted on the y-axis.

whyNot.0: Water temperature is the independent variable, plotted on the x-axis.
whyNot.1: The mass of sugar should be the same in every cup: a controlled variable.
whyNot.3: The water volume should be held constant: a controlled variable.

explain.body: The control group gets no treatment or a placebo and acts as the baseline. Single-blind: subjects do not know their group. Double-blind: neither subjects nor outcome measurers know. Random assignment makes the groups comparable.

test.q: What is the main purpose of giving the control group a placebo?
options: To give the control group a smaller dose
To control for the placebo effect
To make the sample more representative
To let researchers know who got the drug
test.why: A placebo controls for the placebo effect: improvement that comes from believing you are being treated.

whyNot.0: A placebo contains no active drug at all, not a smaller dose.
whyNot.2: Representativeness comes from random sampling, not from a placebo.
whyNot.3: A placebo helps keep subjects (and, in double-blind studies, researchers) unaware of group membership.

explain.body: Reliability is consistency: repeated trials and larger samples improve it. Validity means the study measures what it claims and the conclusion is justified: good controls and a fair test improve it.

test.q: Repeating an experiment many times and getting consistent results mainly demonstrates its:
options: Validity
Accuracy
Reliability
Randomization
test.why: Consistency across repeated trials is reliability.

whyNot.0: Validity is whether the study measures what it claims; a consistent but flawed test can still be invalid.
whyNot.1: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; consistent results can all be wrong by the same amount.
whyNot.3: Randomization is how subjects are assigned, not a property shown by repeating trials.

explain.body: A controlled experiment, where the researcher sets the independent variable, can show cause and effect. Observational, correlational and field studies cannot by themselves; they are used when an experiment would be unethical or impractical.

test.q: Which study design can establish cause and effect?
options: A large observational study
A correlational field survey
A detailed single case study
A controlled experiment
test.why: Only a controlled experiment, where the researcher changes one variable and controls the rest, can establish causation.

whyNot.0: However large, an observational study records what happens without assigning the IV, so it shows association.
whyNot.1: Correlational surveys show variables changing together, not that one causes the other.
whyNot.2: A case study describes one person or event and cannot test cause and effect.
